Meat / Restaurant

Spicy Dwaeji Bulgogi

Dwaeji bulgogi is pork's answer to the bulgogi (#M01) idea, dressed in the yangnyeom lane's red paste: thin pork slices in a gochujang-gochugaru marinade, grilled fast and hot, folded into ssam or heaped over rice.

Korean · Easy · Serves 4

Behind the dish

A PLACE AT
the table.

Stream: restaurant — the gochujang pork lane. Dwaeji bulgogi is pork's answer to the bulgogi (#M01) idea, dressed in the yangnyeom lane's red paste: thin pork slices in a gochujang-gochugaru marinade, grilled fast and hot, folded into ssam or heaped over rice. Where beef bulgogi runs sweet and juicy, its pork cousin runs hot and savory-sweet — the fat of a shoulder slice carries the paste's ferment better than any lean meat could. This is the spice-first workhorse of the Korean grill table, and the record every weeknight cook should own from this site. Name it honestly at your table: it shares architecture with bulgogi, but it is the yangnyeom lane's dish, not soy-slurry bulgogi with a pepper swap. Who cooks what: one grill boss on the batches, the table on ssam — the pork cooks so fast that the assembly line matters more than the fire.

Set yourself up

Before you cook

  • Blend the paste smooth. Gochujang whisked with the soy, honey, and mirin first; then the gochugaru, sesame oil, garlic, ginger, onion, and the squeezed pear. The pear is enzyme and a whisper of fruit, not the sweet engine it is in #M01 — squeeze it dry or the marinade steams instead of chars.
  • Marinate 2–8 hours, refrigerated. Two is honest for a weeknight; the pork's fat protects it where a lean beef would mush, so the window is generous.
  • Plan the heat before you mix, not after. The gochugaru is the dial: 1 tablespoon for a table that says "a little spicy," 2 for the honest default, more for nobody. Gochujang heat builds through the meal — set the dial for bite fifteen, not bite one.
  • Pull the pork out 20 minutes before the fire; cold slices on a hot grate steam gray at the edges.

LET’S make it.

  1. 01
    Fire hot, batches small. Charcoal or cast-iron at a solid medium-high — a pan surface around 200 °C, oil just at the shimmer. The slices go on in one loose layer — piled pork steams in the paste's moisture, and steamed paste is bitter. Single layer, sixty to ninety seconds undisturbed. Checkpoint — the paste should sizzle and darken one shade, and the air should carry toasted chile and sesame. Black edges in the first minute mean the fire is a notch past the paste's tolerance — raise the grate or bank the coals and continue.
  2. 02
    Flip at the weep, pull fast. Turn the slices when the edges bead juice and the underside is brick-brown, 60–90 seconds more on the second side, off the fire while the centers still carry a blush of juice. Pork shoulder at 4 mm is done in under three minutes a batch; every extra ten seconds trades juice for toughness. Checkpoint — test piece at the grill station: glazed edge, juicy-fatty interior, heat arriving after the sweet on the finish. If the center is dry, the batch was thin-spread and overcooked — next batch spends less time on the second side.
  3. 03
    The two ways to eat it, both correct. The ssam way: leaf, thin ssamjang swipe, a hot slice, garlic coin, fold, one bite — the record's full ceremony. The weeknight way: rice in a bowl, a stack of slices over, sesame and scallion, the pan's juice spooned last. Same meat, two speeds. Checkpoint — the bowl test: the juice over rice should be red-gold and savory-sweet, milder than the slices taste plain — if it runs bitter, the pan's sugared drippings caught fire at some point and the heat was a notch high throughout; note it for next time, eat around it now. Chef’s Note — heat honesty for the cook: the paste's capsaicin sits in the oil phase, so sesame oil carries it evenly through the marinade — one more reason the oil goes in measured (a tablespoon, not a pour). At the table, milk or rice tames a bite that ran hot; water walks the heat around your mouth without touching it. Old news to the regulars, news to somebody at every table.

Doneness & Quality Checkpoints

  • The slice: 4 mm against the grain, shoulder or collar, marinated 2–8 hours in a smooth paste.
  • The grill: single loose layer, flip at the beading edge, brick-brown not black, under three minutes a batch.
  • The pull: juicy centers with a blush of juice, never gray-through.
  • The table: ssam or rice-bowl, cold banchan in reach, heat dialed for the end of the meal.

Finish & Plate

Platter at the center, sesame and scallion over the glistening red slices, and the pan's juice scraped into a small bowl for the rice. Ssam leaves, ssamjang (#SA01), garlic coins, and the cold cucumber (#B07) within every hand's reach — this record's table runs hot, and the cold crunch is not optional garnish.

Troubleshooting

SymptomCauseFix
Paste blackened, bitterFire past the paste's toleranceRaise the grate; smaller batches; squeeze the pear drier
Meat dry and grayLoin used, or overcooked on a clockShoulder/collar; pull at the beading edge
Ssam collapses, soggyWet leaves or overloaded foldBone-dry lettuce; one slice, one garlic coin
Heat arrived before the flavorGochugaru over-dialed for the jar's own heatTaste the gochujang plain before mixing; 1 tbsp to start
Bland despite red colorMarinate under 2 hoursThe window is the flavor; 2 hours minimum

Storage, Make-Ahead & Variations

  • Marinated pork keeps 24 hours (freeze flat up to a month). Cooked, 3 days — and the leftovers are arguably the record's second life: kimchi fried rice with diced dwaeji bulgogi, or a melt-grade cheese-and-dwaeji quesadilla that the fusion lane would claim if it could.
  • Variations: the same paste on pork belly slabs (#M11's slower cousin); on chicken thighs (#M17); thinned with mirin into a glaze for the shrimp record (#SF01). The soy-pork fork without heat is ganjang pork bulgogi (#M14).
